title: The Complete Guide to LLM Evaluation
story_key: story|title:the complete guide to llm evaluation
content_excerpt: In this article, you will learn how to evaluate LLM applications systematically, from choosing scorers and designing reliable LLM judges to evaluating RAG systems and agents across the release cycle. You test most LLM apps by reading a few outputs and deciding they look fine. A prompt edit, a model swap, or a retrieval change then breaks something you never checked. And by then you can’t quite tell which change caused it. LLM evaluation catches these breaks before users do. You build test cases, score each output against written criteria, and compare scores before and after every change. It is the regression-testing loop from regular code, adapted for outputs that differ on every run. LLM outputs vary between runs, and “correct” depends on context. A unit test asserts equality, but “You can return shoes within 30 days” and “Returns are accepted for a month after delivery” are both right, and no string comparison knows it. If you block deployment on a faithfulness score of 0.7, you will argue about an arbitrary threshold every week. Use evaluation to guide iteration and tests to protect the release. Every eval has three parts: a dataset of inputs, scorers that grade outputs, and a record of scores over time. The rest of this article builds on these. A scorer takes a test case (input, output, and sometimes context or a reference) and returns a verdict or a number. There are three categories, as shown below: Overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE count shared n-grams with a reference , so a correct paraphrase scores low. Embedding-based scores such as BERTScore handle paraphrase through cosine similarity between token embeddings, but they need a reference and cannot judge tone or whether a claim is supported by a source. Start with code scorers wherever a rule works. They cost nothing and return the same result every time. Add a judge only for the criteria that rules cannot express. An LLM judge is a model prompted to grade another model’s output. Its job is narrower than generation: it reads a rubric and a candidate answer, then emits a verdict. Three setups cover most uses: The rubric is the whole product. A usable judge prompt has four parts: a definition of the criterion, the inputs the judge may use, a procedure, and a strict output format. Vague criteria like “is the answer good” produce vague scores. Compare that with this faithfulness judge for a policy-answering bot: call_llm is your own function that sends a prompt to a model and returns text. Three

title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency
summary: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.

title: Paper-Faithful Federated Learning: Scientific Checks for Practitioner and Agent Development
summary: Federated learning experiments can produce reasonable-looking results even when the experiment implementation differs from the intended experimental protocol. Small errors in configuration, data partitioning, aggregation, randomness, evaluation, or checkpoint recovery may therefore affect a comparison without causing the program to fail. We present FedBrew, a research codebase for controlled and reproducible federated learning experiments. Its focus is controlled simulation with checks of specified conditions of the intended experimental protocol. FedBrew uses configuration checks, identifiable client data partitions, checkpoint recovery checks, self-describing run records, and development-time checks of scientific conditions. These checks assess, for example, whether client partitions are disjoint and exhaustive and aggregation weights match the prescribed rule; numerical and recovery checks examine non-finite client model states and interrupted runs. The same structure also provides clear extension points and automated checks for new algorithms, datasets, models, and tasks, whether they are added by researchers or AI coding agents. FedBrew therefore supports reproducible and inspectable FL experiments through checks of specified software and scientific conditions and the run records associated with reported results.

title: LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds
summary: We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic environment platform for LLM agents, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating reliable decision-making in real-world geographic environments using GeoWorld. Unlike existing evaluations that largely reason and plan over fixed geographic states, GeoWorld is grounded in real-world geographic structure and allows external world states to evolve along their own temporal processes while preserving verifiable state histories. LiveGeo places geographic tasks within this evolving environment, requiring agents to actively acquire task-relevant information, verify whether the evidence supporting prior decisions remains valid, and revise their plans when necessary. Our results reveal that even frontier LLMs struggle with static tasks, with no model consistently excelling across tasks, while strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability. Further analysis identifies a key bottleneck: agents struggle to acquire and translate relevant evidence into valid decisions and maintain their correctness as the world evolves. By releasing LiveGeo together with its GeoWorld platform, we aim to provide the community with a flexible and extensible infrastructure for studying the next generation of agents capable of reliable action in evolving geographic worlds.

title: Rethinking Memory for AI Inference
content_excerpt: Processing data closer to memory could reduce power and boost performance, but software, thermal, and architectural challenges remain. The shift from AI training in data centers to AI inferencing at the edge will require a fundamental rethinking of where and how data is processed and stored, how it is prioritized, and what needs to be traded off in terms of power and performance to stay within a limited power budget. At the center of these efforts is a recognition that the explosion of data — especially in physical AI where data is being live-streamed from sensors — requires much of that data to be processed as close to memory as possible. This has been a topic of discussion since the inception of the Internet of Things, but it really began gaining traction with AI due to the flood of data and concerns about the amount of power required to move and process it. In battery-electric vehicles and drones, for example, the less energy spent on processing data, the greater the range per charge and the more energy that can be allocated to critical and not-so-critical functions. The challenge is understanding what data needs to be kept, what can be discarded, and what needs to be acted upon. Those are very different priorities. Making those choices requires advanced processing, and the quickest path to results using the least amount of energy is to minimize the distance data needs to travel between processing and memory. “The realities of these LLMs getting into physical devices are causing everyone to rethink how they architect their memory,” said Frank Ferro, group director for product management at Cadence . “Even with conventional memory — without even talking about processing in memory — how do I partition these models to maximize the performance both of the overall processor and memory subsystem?” Solving those issues will require several new approaches, such as processing near memory (PNM) and processing in memory (PIM), as well as improvements across multiple technologies and approaches. Compilers and operating systems will need to catch up, and standards will need to be established. “AI in the data center and all these large language models have been the focus of everyone’s attention for the last couple of years, and now these models have been trained and pushed out into the field, into the edge of the network and physical AI,” Ferro said. “The reality is you have limited compute power and limited memory.” AI inferencing at the edge presents different chal

title: What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents
summary: Eval-driven development helps you build AI agents against a consistent set of metrics. Define good behavior, write the eval first, then compare experiments.
story_key: story|title:what is eval driven development how to improve ai agents
content_excerpt: Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse. Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench ), and have boiled it down to a three step process: In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process. The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic: As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it ( LLM-as-a-judge ). With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them. The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent. EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. Before writing code, it’s helpful to define a short spec that covers: Say we have an internal docs agent that employees query for company information. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets. title: When Both Sides Adapt: The Challenges of Evaluating Interactive LLM Systems
summary: In interactive systems where users engage with LLMs, users are adaptive and, after observing LLM responses, can change their prompting strategy, as well as the type and difficulty of subsequent tasks. Thus model responses can influence the set of prompts on which the model is subsequently evaluated. We study the implications of this user adaptivity and prompt endogeneity for the evaluation of LLMs. We define two classes of estimands for comparing models: the common-distribution effect, which compares model performance on the same distribution of prompts, and the induced-distribution effect, which compares each model on the prompt distribution generated through user interaction. We show that offline benchmark evaluation and live A/B testing target different quantities, with the standard difference-in-means estimators for the two methods converging to the common-distribution effect and the induced-distribution effect, respectively. This distinction can affect decision-making: the two comparisons can rank models differently and lead to discrepancies in deployment recommendations. We characterize when such ranking reversals occur and provide a sufficient condition under which the rankings are guaranteed to agree. This result provides a practical heuristic for assessing whether offline evaluation is sufficient to reproduce the decision suggested by a live experiment. Third, we show, in a stylized linear model of interactions, that user adaptivity can increase variance in estimation. Finally, we discuss implications of user adaptivity for the interpretation of experiments and show that adaptivity creates a common mechanism leading to common evaluation challenges, such as reward hacking and novelty effects. Together, this work highlights the necessity of measuring both model performance as well as changes in the user behavior that the model induces.

title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
